newsitem.title: GAMBIA: Gambians stock up supplies ahead of poll.
newsitem.headline: Gambians stock up supplies ahead of poll.

text.p: Residents of Gambia's capital Banjul besieged shops on Tuesday to stock up, two days before presidential elections marred by campaign violence.
The government has declared a two-day holiday in the tiny West African state from polling day on Thursday and paid civil servants their September salaries.

After a bruising two-week campaign period, many Gambians are apprehensive of the outcome of the election designed to end two years of army rule. Religious leaders have called for prayers and Christians have been asked to fast.
In the most serious incident, military leader Colonel Yahya Jammeh's motorcade was pelted with stones as it ran the gauntlet of a hostile opposition crowd outside the capital on Sunday.
Jammeh was not harmed but his main civilian challenger, lawyer Ousainon Darboe, said soldiers used the occasion to beat up his own supporters. He said 36 had been taken to hospital.
"They brutalised my supporters and seized some of their cars," said Darboe, leader of the United Democratic Party (UDP), at a news conference on Monday.
Darboe, vice-president of the Gambia Bar Association, accused the army of backing Jammeh, who seized power in a 1994 coup and left the army in August to seek a popular manadate.
He said Jammeh had politicised the army, police and National Intelligence Agency, with their heads sporting Jammeh badges.
Many Gambians say the race between Jammeh 31, and Darboe, 48 appeared too close to call.
"It is difficult to know by the turnout of the crowds at the rallies who will win between the two," said a local journalist.
Jammeh has the clear advantage of virtual monopoly of state media, notably television, non-existent in Gambia until he set up a government network after his coup.
He gets about four hours of television exposure daily -- probably longer for state radio. Darboe and the two other opposition candidates are virtually excluded form state media.
The government justified this by saying they had misused their broadcast time by abusing Jammeh.

Darboe is from the Mandinka tribe of ousted president Sir Dawda Jawara, who account for 40 percent of the population of just over one million. Jammeh is from the minority Jola, who are only 10 percent of the population.
Jammeh, a devout Moslem, has been trying to broaden his electoral base by reaching out to traditional religious authorities in the predominantly Islamic state.
Distribution of free copies of the Holy Koran is a regular feature of Jammeh's campaign rallies.

In his final campaign speeches, Jammeh asked Gambians to judge him by his record in bringing Gambians modern amenities like television and a new airport terminal under construction as well as hospitals, schools and improved electricity supply.
Darboe pledged to stop the increasing use of Gambia as a transit nation for the drug trade, which he said was damaging the country's image abroad.
"We don't want Gambia to become another Panama," he said in a speech broadcast on a private radio station.
The electoral law set the end of campaigning at midnight on Tuesday.
The other presidentianl contenders are Sidia Jatta of the small People's Democratic Organisation for Independence and Socialism, who stood against Jawara in 1992, and hotel manager Amath Bah.
